name: Amparo Purple
lede: Amparo Purple is a bright, medium purple recorded in Ridgway's 1912 atlas, and nearly identical in the color graph to a library entry with a completely different name.

sections.title: A name in the library
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature places this hue on plate XI, hue 63, tone b [1]. Maerz and Paul's dictionary independently dates a swatch to 1912 as well, with no plate number recorded [1]. The name itself is undocumented in the sources consulted; "Amparo" is a Spanish word for shelter and a common given name, but no source here confirms a connection [1].

The color graph's nearest match is striking: [[orchid-purple]] sits at a computed distance of 0.0, effectively the same color under a different name [2]. [[light-hortense-violet]], named for the hydrangea (*Hortensia*), is close behind at 2.7 units, with [[lavender-floral]] and [[floral-lavender]] further out at 4.1, and [[soft-purple]] beyond that [2]. Munsell gives 6.0P 5.8/12.4, a purple of high chroma and medium lightness [1]. The hex #B775CA is a screen approximation of the Ridgway plate [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: At a looser match (ΔE 15), our archive finds this purple in 69 of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, about 0.3 percent [3]. The strongest matches are marine scenes under stormy or evening light: Eugène Boudin's *Voiliers* (1869), Ludolf Bakhuysen's *A Seascape with Figures by a Boat on a Shore* (1667), and Claude Monet's *The Beach at Sainte-Adresse* (1867) [3]. The cluster of ships and shorelines under this purple-grey light is a pattern in the matches themselves, not a documented painter's choice [3]. All matches are computed on photographed, varnished canvases [3].
